title: Developed nations must bear much of the cost of carbon emissions
content_html:
COP31 ended in Antalya, Türkiye, with a whimper. The 190-odd countries that had convened for nearly 12 days — a close to 50-hour overshoot — failed to agree on an overarching political statement, called a cover text, that acts as a stepping stone to future, collective global action on climate change. Usually, cover texts evolve as a final synthesis of deliberations; the COP31 leadership, helmed by Türkiye and Australia, thought it fit to push for a cover text early in the proceedings. The headline sought was a global electrification target: 35% of global final energy consumption will come from electricity by 2035, in the hope that this would reduce direct fossil fuel emissions. Ultimately, the cover text failed to pass muster because the European Union objected to the text’s lack of any explicit mention of ‘fossil fuel,’ let alone its phase-out. The COP process is arduously protracted as even a single country’s objection can stall progress. Country-blocks outside the EU, such as coalitions of the least developed countries, island nations, some South American countries — reportedly 130 countries — were also insistent on fossil fuel language. While COP 31 made some progress on old pathways, such as the Just Transition agreement, it is perplexing that the delegations could not make progress on the other big prong of negotiations: climate finance.

The increase in solar panel installations and the significant shift towards battery use in grid storage and transport did not come cheap: the cost of the land required for their installation, their intermittent nature of being dependent on weather, grid upgrades all carry costs. It is global markets, imperfectly connected, but connected, that have managed to bring it to this stage over decades. India and China, major fossil emitters, with large, still indigent populations, are also leaders in total clean energy installations. Therefore it stands to reason that developed countries, which have committed to providing climate finance in recognition of their historical emissions, make good on past promises to shoulder the cost of the carbon emissions that are responsible for warming. Economic crises are a feature, and not a bug, of the interconnected financial system enveloping the world and there are, undeniably, challenges to diverting the necessary finance towards countries most vulnerable to climate change impact. However, it is no longer prudent to sweep this under the rug by scuttling experimental approaches — namely carbon capture — as inimical to the broader commitment to eschew fossil fuel. When the primary framework climate agreement was crafted three decades ago, nobody envisaged AI and the drain that data centres portended or the wars that would see the vociferous antagonists of coal immediately shore up their gas reserves. Without honest good-faith dialogue, the COP is at risk of being a sideshow: a mortal blow to multilateralism.

title: Rohingya cannot return unless Myanmar turns democratic
content_html:
On November 19, the International Court of Justice held that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya. It is for the first time that the court has found any state responsible for the crime. The verdict, with nine votes to six, was not lightly reached. Genocide requires proof of an intent to destroy a group. In the absence of direct evidence of a plan, the court could infer that intent only if it was “the only reasonable inference” from the facts, a high bar to affix responsibility. The facts it accepted are harrowing. In 2017, in what Myanmar’s army called “clearance operations” against the insurgent Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army, at least 10,000 Rohingya were killed, 1,834 raped and 392 villages destroyed in northern Rakhine State. Over 7,00,000 fled to Bangladesh. Then Army chief Min Aung Hlaing, now Myanmar’s “civilian” President, called the “Bengali problem” an “unfinished job”. Myanmar argued that it had only been fighting insurgents or at worst, driving the Rohingya out or punishing them. The court said that the army drew no distinction between fighters and civilians, had no plan to move anyone, fired on fleeing people and killed children on a scale that could not be explained as punishment. Seen alongside decades of discrimination, the evidence pointed to an intent to destroy.

The incidents of 2017 were no aberration. The army drove lakhs of Rohingya into Bangladesh in 1978 and 1991-92. The junta stripped the Rohingya of citizenship in 1982 and the state branded them as “foreigners” in Arakan, disenfranchising them in 2015. While the junta’s Bamar-Buddhist vision has oppressed every minority, the Rohingya have been subjected to the most brutality. More than 1.2 million are in Bangladesh, living in dilapidated conditions, made worse due to diminished international aid. The court ordered Myanmar to allow their safe, voluntary and dignified return and to compensate them, but it has no means of enforcing its judgment. Only the UN Security Council can, but it will be subject to vetoes by Myanmar’s backers, China and Russia. On the very day of the verdict, the two joined the U.S. in Shenzhen to declare the “immunities of State officials” of “paramount importance”. Others, India among them, have courted the regime in Naypyitaw regardless, following sham elections that made the junta leader civilian President earlier this year. And Rakhine State, mired in civil war, is now mostly held by the Arakan Army which is accused of atrocities against the Rohingya. Only a truly democratic, federal, plural and peaceful Myanmar can bring the Rohingya home in safety.

title: Don’t use language to divide people
author: T. Ramakrishnan
content_html:
The Tamil Nadu government has a “once in a lifetime” opportunity to bring a paradigm shift in its two-language policy as it has one more month to decide on its stand in the Navodaya schools case, which is pending before the Supreme Court. The case is about the State government having to allot land in every district for Jawahar Navodaya Vidyalayas (JNVs), which are residential co-educational schools run by the Union government in rural areas.

Ever since the launch of the JNVs in 1985-86, the Tamil Nadu government, irrespective of the party in power, has been opposing it on the grounds that these schools come with a three-language formula, which goes against the State government’s traditional two-language policy. Most political parties in the State contend that the three-language formula is a ruse to “reintroduce” Hindi, which was scrapped by the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) government as a language of learning in State syllabus schools in 1968.

title: A framework for nuclear risk reduction cannot wait
author: Adya  Madhavan
content_html:
For the first time since 1972, there is no treaty formally restricting the world’s largest nuclear arsenals. New START (New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty) expired in February, and nine months later, a successor treaty is still far from being drafted. Russia had offered to keep observing New START’s limits for a year if the United States did the same. Instead, the U.S. has pushed for an “improved” agreement, insisting that any nuclear treaty must involve China, which understandably has its own reservations.

On November 19, the leaders of the three countries met for the first time on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen. They issued a joint declaration reaffirming that a nuclear war must never be fought. They also pledged subsequent talks on reducing nuclear risks and preventing proliferation. However, there are no provisions for the verification of compliance with these commitments, and no date seems to have been fixed for further talks. Despite Shenzhen, the underlying tension between the three countries’ positions remains. Each country’s position makes sense from where it sits, but at a time fraught with conflict, further complicated by emerging technologies, this treaty-less scenario cannot continue indefinitely.

title: At COP31, India asked who gets to develop on a warming planet
author: Suman  Chandra
content_html:
The Antalya talks ended without a cover decision titled the Antalya pact. But the drafts show why India’s insistence on historical responsibility, climate finance, and adaptation belongs at the centre of any credible plan to cut emissions.

The priorities of the CoP31 Presidency from the beginning were some signals to the world for climate action which included the target of “35 by 35 electrification”, or raising electricity’s share of global final energy consumption to 35% by 2035. A percentage can make climate diplomacy look deceptively simple. But without a nuance to the conversation, it is difficult to grasp what it takes to, for example, electrify a factory where the grid is unreliable, or to make electric cooking affordable for a low-income household.

Given the different starting points for different nations, the same global percentage can look starkly different. India’s nuanced approach brought those differentiations which ensue directly from the Convention and its Paris Agreement back to the centre of the conversation. As Parties worked through the various iterations of what came to be called the draft Antalya pact, the contextualisation within the finance, technology, and different capacities of countries to deliver it came front and centre.

With disproportionate focus on the Presidency-led cover text and abysmal focus on mandated agenda items, the political package eluded consensus at the closing plenary on November 22. Parties’ divergences emerged on key elements of top-down quantified targets, disregard for overshoot of 1.5 degrees Celsius, and absence of any serious consideration of adaptation needs and climate finance that is disbursed.

Parties did adopt separate decisions, including on the Global Goal on Adaptation, Adaptation Fund, and Just Transition Work Programme. India’s constructive role was to provide bridging language and eventually get a text which addressed these concerns at the closing plenary.

title: Letters to The Editor — November 24, 2026
content_html:
COP31 outcome

The collapse of consensus at the Antalya summit — despite running into overtime — highlights the deep divide stalling global climate action as the world faces breaching the 1.5°C warming limit. While over 130 nations rightfully opposed diluting fossil fuel phase-out commitments, India’s stance that climate ambition must match the means of implementation is valid. Developing economies cannot compromise their energy security without assured climate finance and technology transfer from historically responsible, developed nations. Without honouring common but differentiated responsibilities alongside clear transition pathways, future summits will remain trapped in stalemate.

title: The Bilkis Bano order — justice deferred again
author: Faizan Mustafa,Aashank Dwivedi
content_html:
“Justice is the first virtue of social institutions, as truth is of systems of thought,” said John Rawls in A Theory of Justice. The American political philosopher’s line is easy to admire yet hard to practice. When an institution cannot be trusted to hear a wronged person, the old maxim justice delayed is justice denied begins to sound less like a warning than a description.

For nearly a quarter of a century, Bilkis Bano, a survivor of the 2002 Gujarat riots who was gang-raped by 11 men while pregnant and lost some members of her family, has had to prove over and over again what happened to her was real, that it was a crime, and that the law should answer it. Each time, she has done so with a defiant courage that has become a testament to the Republic’s conscience. She now may have to do it again. On October 28, 2026, a Supreme Court Bench of Justices M.M. Sundresh and Prasanna B. Varale suspended the life sentences of two of the 11 men convicted of gang-raping her and murdering some members of her family, granting them bail pending their appeals. Ms. Bano told the media that she learnt of the order just a few days ago through the press. The counsel for the two men later issued a statement on November 21, rejecting Ms. Bano’s allegation that she was kept in the dark about the proceedings but asserting that she was not party even in High Court.

“It is still baffling to me that for the second time after this order was passed, I have not been summoned to appear before the Supreme Court, nor has anything been heard from me,” Ms. Bano said in a statement through her attorneys. It is a sentence that no citizen, for whatever reason he may have for taking the oath regardless of his opinion of the merits of the order, should find easy to read.

Every word counts here. This case is designed to elicit both outrage and defensive responses. No one is found “not guilty” in the order. The principles, which were upheld by the Bombay High Court in 2017, remain the same. What the Bench has done is that it has merely suspended the sentences of the two men, Bipinchand Kanhaiyalal Joshi and Pradip Ramanlal Modhiya, until their appeals are disposed of, by pointing out that both men have been in jail for over 17 years, one of them has a severe disability, and their appeals raise questions of fact and law that require examination. The Additional Solicitor General opposed the pleas. The convicts’ appeals against the High Court’s judgment are still to be decided.

There is no objection to the order in the context of not subscribing to retributive or deterrent theories of punishment. However, at a time when there is talk of making the criminal justice system victim-centric, why was victimology forgotten in this case? That is the central question which survives despite the November 23, 2026 order by the same Bench releasing Siraj Pada, one of the convicts of the Sabarmati Express coach fire on similar grounds.

title: Core accountability: On core sector performance
content_html:
The core sector performance in October is a good example of how statistical distortions can create incorrect assessments of the economy. The 10.9% growth rate, a series high, has been celebrated as a sign of the Indian economy’s strength and resilience. There is, no doubt, an aspect of this has been reflected in the numbers, especially to do with infrastructure creation. However, the much more impactful factor behind the high core sector growth was a low base effect. The overall Index of Core Industries grew just 0.8% in October 2025 and so, in relation, the performance in October 2026 looked that much faster. This low base effect is even starker when looking at individual sectors within the index. The coal sector grew at a blistering 23% in October, more than twice its growth rate in the previous month. Yet, a large part of this was propelled by the fact that the sector had contracted nearly 8.5% last October. The rest of the sector’s growth was driven by demand of the electricity and iron ore sectors, or so the data show. The electricity sector also grew at a series high of nearly 22% in October, but on the back of a near-7% contraction in October last year. This base effect anomaly is likely down to the fact that the festive season starts at different but similar points every year. As such, a more accurate reading of the economy will be possible once the data for November are available.

The construction-related sectors seem to have seen genuine growth, a reflection of the government’s ongoing infrastructure push. The iron ore sector’s growth rate accelerated to a three-month high of 26.4% in October 2026 as compared to a growth of 8.7% in the same month last year. Steel grew at 7.3% versus 9.5% last year, and cement by 15.4% versus 5.2%. The economy’s dependence on government spending is not going to ease in the near future, and might even intensify as higher costs eat into companies’ profit margins. The core sector data once again highlighted a major reason for these higher costs — the oil and gas sectors. The crude oil sector shrank by 4.1%, its 22nd consecutive month of contraction. The natural gas sector, similarly, contracted 7.6%, a series-worst performance and the 28th straight month of contraction. A major reason behind high inflation in India is the underperformance of these two sectors and the resultant dependence on imported fuel. It is time the Petroleum Ministry candidly explains — to Parliament in December or to the public directly — why India’s fuel output has been continuously falling. If it is a matter of a lack of resources underground, that is one thing, but the underperformance of oil and gas public sector undertakings is quite another. Accountability needs to be set.

Steel grew at 7.3% versus 9.5% last year, and cement by 15.4% versus 5.2%. The economy’s dependence on government spending is not going to ease in the near future, and might even intensify as higher costs eat into companies’ profit margins. The core sector data once again highlighted a major reason for these higher costs — the oil and gas sectors. The crude oil sector shrank by 4.1%, its 22nd consecutive month of contraction. The natural gas sector, similarly, contracted 7.6%, a series-worst performance and the 28th straight month of contraction. A major reason behind
high inflation in India
is the underperformance of these two sectors and the resultant dependence on imported fuel. It is time the Petroleum Ministry candidly explains — to Parliament in December or to the public directly — why India’s fuel output has been continuously falling. If it is a matter of a lack of resources underground, that is one thing, but the underperformance of oil and gas public sector undertakings is quite another. Accountability needs to be set.
